Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event
Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

vignette: Two years prior, Aroha deployed to a fractured region as a relief worker. One afternoon, the perimeter collapsed. Shrapnel tore through the distribution hub, and Aroha pressed into the dirt as the ground shook. A canteen ruptured nearby, spilling a bitter, metallic powder that coated her tongue, a flavor that clung to her despite the falling rain. She moved through the wreckage helping the injured, her attention repeatedly drawn to faces marked by devastation—babies wrapped in torn blankets, elders who would never speak again, and a young man whose eyes remained fixed even as he stopped breathing. When panicked locals began shouting, their voices rising in sharp, urgent tones, Aroha felt her chest tighten. She remembered the sound of boots on gravel, but whenever she tried to reconstruct the hours afterward, the pieces refused to align. In the months that followed, Aroha noticed how her own mind fractured around the event. When she sat alone attempting to rebuild what happened that day, she would reach for a particular moment and find nothing but an empty wall. Whole stretches of time simply vanished from her recollection, no matter how hard she strained. She would sit on the edge of her bed, hands pressed to her temples, trying to deliberately pull the past forward. Yet the edges of the recollection kept dissolving before they could fully form, as though an invisible hand pushed the memory away just as she neared it. She stopped asking colleagues for details. The gaps were not forgotten; they were simply absent. Today, Aroha works as a parole officer, spending her mornings in a cramped, fluorescent-lit office. During afternoon intake meetings, she sits across from clients who shift their posture and let their voices drop into low, steady warnings. Aroha has come to understand that the slightest shift in tone—a clipped syllable, a calm but firm expression of anger—sends a cold current through her nervous system. She adjusts her folder and steers the conversation back to paperwork. When she reviews case files, photographs of clients occasionally surface, and the sight of a child’s face suddenly pulls her back to the faces she could not save. She keeps the blinds drawn during those moments, focusing entirely on administrative language until her hands stop trembling. Sometimes, when a colleague offers her bitter chicory coffee, the exact taste floods her mouth, and she sets the mug down without a word. Aroha did not come to therapy because she felt broken. She came because the silence in her apartment had grown too loud, and the way she braced herself at every parole meeting was beginning to fray her concentration. She divorced her husband six months ago, not from conflict, but from the quiet realization that she could no longer share a bed without flinching at his breathing. Now, she sits across from you, her shoulders slightly hunched, her gaze fixed on the table. She is afraid that the gaps in her memory will widen until nothing remains, that the triggers will eventually cross a threshold she cannot cross back from. What she hopes for is simply to stop fighting her own mind, to find a way to carry the weight of what happened without it dictating every conversation. She wants to remember, not to be haunted, but to finally rest.
